To study about the permissions in JIRA.

PERMISSIONS
Permissions are settings within Jira applications that control what users within those applications can see and do. All Jira applications allow a variety of permissions, from whether users can create new projects to whether a user can see a specific type of comment on an issue. These permissions can differ between applications.

TYPES OF PERMISSIONS
There are three types of permissions in Jira applications, ranging from high-level to granular:
Global permissions – Apply to the application as a whole, not individual projects (e.g., whether users can see other users in the application).
Project permissions – Organized into permission schemes; apply to projects (e.g., who can see the project's issues, create, edit, and assign them).
Issue security permissions – Organized into security schemes; allow visibility of individual issues to be adjusted within the bounds of the project's permissions.
Log in to the Jira site.
Click the gear icon (Settings) → select System.
Under Security in the left sidebar, click Global permissions to view the list of global permissions and the groups assigned to each.
Open a project → click Project settings → Permissions to view the permission scheme applied to that project, showing which roles can browse, create, edit, and assign issues.
If available on the plan, go to Project settings → Issue security to view or configure issue-level security schemes.
Take screenshots of the Global Permissions page and the Project Permissions page.

Filter Results Gadget - displays a team's task board-style view, showing items from the current sprint with their status and assignee, useful for daily stand-ups.

Reporting in Jira involves gaining knowledge about the health, progress, and overall status of projects through project reports, dashboard gadgets, and filter-based views. Every space automatically offers standard reports without additional configuration. Current Jira Cloud groups these under a project's Reports tab, and includes:

In addition, Dashboard gadgets provide reporting at a personal or team level, including: Activity Stream, Assigned to Me, Average Age Chart, Filter Results, Pie Chart, Sprint Health, Issue/Work Item Statistics, and Two-Dimensional Filter Statistics.
Log in to Jira.
Open the required Scrum or Kanban space.
Click the Reports tab in the space's navigation.
Select a report type from the list, e.g., Sprint Report, Burndown Chart, or Velocity Chart.
Choose the sprint or date range to generate the report for.
View the report's visual output — line graphs, bar charts, or tables depending on the report type.
Navigate to Dashboards → Create dashboard for additional gadget-based reporting.
Add gadgets such as Pie Chart, Filter Results, or Average Age Chart, and configure each with the required project/filter.
Save the dashboard.
Verify the reports reflect accurate, up-to-date data for the project.

To study about sprint retrospective items in Jira.
DESCRIPTION:

Agile retrospectives are not "post-mortem" meetings held only at project end — they occur at the close of every sprint throughout the project's lifetime. A retrospective is key to a product's incremental value and to a team's continuous improvement. Without regular retrospectives, issues cannot be fixed before they grow into larger problems, and teams lose out on Agile's long-term benefits. In current Jira, retrospectives are conducted through a Confluence whiteboard or page, launched directly from Jira when a sprint completes, keeping the retrospective linked to the sprint's actual data.
Set the Stage — creates a "safe space" for open sharing. Jira/Confluence is a natural venue since all sprint information is already present, making it easy to reference during the session.
Gather Data — team members input ideas independently rather than aloud one at a time, avoiding "groupthink," where the first opinion shared biases everyone else's response.
Generate Insights — the team filters and votes on which topics matter most, prioritizing what to address first. Voting can be configured to limit votes per person and per topic.

Decide What to Do — the most important and most often skipped stage. The output must be a concrete action item, not a vague statement, and should take the form of a Jira work item so it can be tracked and followed up on.

Close the Retrospective — the team formally or informally agrees on the action items and assigns an owner responsible for ensuring the action gets done (not necessarily the person performing the task).
Log in to Jira and open the required Scrum space.
Complete the active sprint (Board → Complete sprint), as retrospectives are typically triggered at sprint close.
When prompted, select the option to create a Sprint Retrospective in Confluence (as a whiteboard or page).
Choose a whiteboard for real-time collaborative input, or a page for a structured written retrospective.
Set the stage by inviting the team and briefly outlining the retrospective's purpose.
Gather data by having each team member independently add ideas/sticky notes under categories such as "What went well," "What didn't go well," and "Ideas for improvement."
Generate insights by grouping similar ideas and voting on the most important topics to discuss.
Decide what to do by converting the top-voted insights into concrete action items, and create corresponding Jira work items for tracking.
Assign an owner to each action item.
Close the retrospective with team agreement, and link the retrospective back to the completed sprint for future reference.
RESULT:
Thus, sprint retrospective items were studied and demonstrated successfully in Jira.
To set up Planning Poker integration in Jira using a Marketplace app.
DESCRIPTION:

Planning poker, also known as "scrum poker" or "pointing poker," is a gamified estimation technique where development teams collectively guess the effort of project tasks. Estimates are based on group consensus rather than individual judgment, making them more engaging and statistically more accurate. Planning Poker is not a native Jira feature — it is available through Marketplace apps (such as Planning Poker for Jira, Actioned, or similar tools) that integrate with Jira via OAuth/application links rather than the older manual "Application Links" configuration used in Server/Data Center versions.
Group estimates from planning poker are statistically higher accuracy than individual guesses.
Helps estimate tasks relative to one another rather than in absolute units.
Identifies gaps between requirements and implementation understanding early.
PROCEDURE:
(Current Jira Cloud):
Log in to Jira as an administrator.
Go to the Atlassian Marketplace (Settings → Apps → Find new apps, or directly via marketplace.atlassian.com).
Search for a Planning Poker app (e.g., "Planning Poker for Jira").
Click Get it now / Try it free to install the app to your Jira site.
Once installed, open the app from the Apps menu in the top navigation.
Follow the app's in-product setup wizard to connect it to your Jira site — modern apps use OAuth-based authorization rather than manually creating Application Links.
Grant the requested permissions when prompted (this replaces the older "Incoming Authentication" configuration step).
Confirm the connection is active by checking the app's dashboard shows your Jira site as linked.
Proceed to create a new estimation game (covered in Part 2).
RESULT:
Thus, the Planning Poker integration was set up successfully in Jira.
To conduct a planning poker estimation session using a Planning Poker app in Jira.
DESCRIPTION:

Planning poker is a gamified technique for estimating project tasks through group consensus rather than individual estimation. Estimation accuracy improves over time as planning poker apps refine estimates with continued use. Modern Planning Poker apps pull stories directly from Jira and sync point values back automatically once voting concludes, eliminating manual data entry.
Open the Planning Poker app from the Jira Apps menu (continuing from Part 1's setup).
Authorize the app to access your Jira site if not already done, and click Allow when prompted.
Click Create new game (or equivalent) to start a new estimation session.
Name the session and select the Jira space/board to import work items from.
Import stories/tasks directly from the Jira backlog into the game.
Invite team members to join the session using the game link or in-app invite.
For each imported item, team members select their estimate simultaneously (cards are hidden until everyone has voted).
Reveal all votes at once to avoid bias, and discuss any significant differences in estimates.
Re-vote if needed until the team reaches consensus on a final estimate.
Confirm the final story point value — the app automatically syncs this value back to the corresponding work item's Story point estimate field in Jira.
Estimated Points: (Game Finished)
RESULT:
Thus, planning poker estimation was conducted successfully in Jira.
